It's September 2033. Andrei's app has been officially launched. The BVG has published a press release. Elif (9) tries to read it at Ludwig's and doesn't understand a thing.
Mr Brandt, it says here: “Following the successful completion of the test phase, the launch of the app for all passengers takes place with immediate effect.” What does that mean? That's not German!
Oh yes it is. Bureaucratic German. It's called the nominal style. People in offices love nouns. Let's translate it into normal German, shall we?
OK. “Following the successful completion of the test phase…”
That means: after the app had been tested successfully. See? From “Durchführung” you make a verb: “durchführen” or, more simply, “testen”.
“…the launch of the app for all passengers takes place with immediate effect.”
That means: from now on all passengers can use the app. Done. Twelve words instead of twenty.
Then why don't they just write it like that?

Because then it doesn't sound so important. But seriously: in a newspaper space is tight. With nouns you can pack a lot of information into one sentence. “Bei Verspätungen” is shorter than “Wenn die Bahn zu spät kommt”.
And here: “To improve accessibility, forty stops were rebuilt.”
That's easy: forty stops were rebuilt so that people like me can get on more easily. One of them is ours. With your tree next to it.
So my tree is in the newspaper? Even though they write so complicatedly?
Indirectly. In the nominal style. “As part of the redesign, the planting of a tree by a pupil took place.” That's how an official would write it.
“mo-bi-li-TEHTS-ine-ge-shrenkt”: a long word, take it syllable by syllable.
In official, scientific and press texts, German turns verbs into nouns and subordinate clauses into prepositional phrases. The information becomes denser, but harder to read.
Nachdem man die App getestet hatte, …
beginnen → der Beginn; ankommen → die Ankunft
helfen → die Hilfe; sprechen → die Sprache
fahren → die Fahrt; ankommen → die Ankunft
The subject and the object of the verb become a genitive or “durch + A”:
The BVG launches the app. → the launch of the app by the BVG
The passengers are satisfied. → the satisfaction of the passengers
The adverb becomes an adjective: “erfolgreich testen” → “der erfolgreiche Test”; “schnell reagieren” → “die schnelle Reaktion”.
At B2 you need to understand the nominal style (reading, listening to the news) and use it in moderation in formal writing. In speech it sounds stiff. A good formal text mixes both styles.

Too much nominal style = “Amtsdeutsch”: “Nach erfolgter Prüfung der Unterlagen erfolgt die Zusendung des Bescheids.” Even Germans laugh at it. The better version: “Nachdem wir Ihre Unterlagen geprüft haben, schicken wir Ihnen den Bescheid.”
After the launch of the app
Before the departure of the train

On the first of September 2033, a grey Thursday, at half past six in the morning, Leo Brandt stood in front of the gate of the Lichtenberg depot and waited. He had come twenty minutes early. He was wearing a new navy-blue jacket with the yellow BVG logo, which had been sent to him the day before, and on the jacket, right over his heart, a small old brass badge with a tram and the letters “BVB”. His grandfather had said: only pin it on in September. Leo had waited until midnight, until it was officially September.

His mother had woken him at five, although he was already awake, and had made him a breakfast he couldn't eat. His father had taken him to the S-Bahn, in silence, and on the platform Thomas suddenly said: “I'm proud of you. I wanted to tell you that before you go. Not only when you finish.” Leo had nodded and said nothing, because he couldn't get a sound out. Only on the S-Bahn, among tired commuters and pupils with headphones, did he understand why his father had said it today of all days: he didn't want to make the same mistake as his own father, back then, at the window.

Next to him stood eleven other trainees, two women and nine men, between seventeen and forty-nine years old. A former baker from Neukölln, who at forty-four had decided to do something completely new once more. A young woman from Ghana, who had been a bus driver in Accra. A student who had dropped out of his philosophy degree because, as he put it, he wanted “to finally do something useful”. They didn't talk much. They were all looking at the gate, behind which, in the early dawn, the long yellow trams stood, row after row, like sleeping animals.

At seven the gate opened, and Kurt Wolff came out, with his old camera round his neck and a clipboard in his hand. He greeted each of them individually, with a handshake, and when he got to Leo, his gaze rested on the badge for a moment. He said nothing. But he nodded, barely visibly, and Leo knew he had recognised it. Then Wolff gave a short speech, and Leo noticed at once that it was different from the press release he had read the evening before. No “erfolgt”. No “Durchführung”. No “Inbetriebnahme”.
Behind them the sun was slowly rising, and the first trams were leaving the depot with a soft hum.

Welcome. In three years you will be driving trams through this city. You will take people to work, to school, to hospital, home. You will drive at night, when everyone is asleep, and in the morning, when everyone is tired. And every day you will make one decision, a thousand times over: do I leave now or do I wait a bit longer? The man who taught me this always used to say: when in doubt, you wait. The timetable is important. The person is more important.

Leo looked at the ground and bit his lip. He knew who Wolff was talking about. The others didn't. The young woman from Ghana standing next to him whispered: “Who was he, the man who taught him that?” Leo hesitated. Then he said quietly: “My grandfather.” The woman looked at him in surprise, then smiled. “Then you're lucky,” she said. “You have someone you can ask.”

At lunch break, in the depot canteen, over a plate of pea soup, Abena told him that she had been living in Berlin for two years. In Accra she had driven a bus for ten years, on one of the busiest routes in the city, through a market where the women traders laid out their goods right on the street. “Compared to that, Berlin is quiet,” she said and laughed. “But the language! Back home you just say: the bus is late. Here it says on the display board: Due to an operational disruption, delays are occurring in the flow of traffic. It took me three months to understand that sentence.” Leo laughed too. He hadn't fully understood it either until today.

The first day was full of forms, safety rules and terms Leo had never heard before. In the afternoon they were allowed into the simulator for the first time: a real driver's cab, rebuilt down to the last screw, in front of a big screen on which the streets of Berlin passed by. Leo sat down in the driver's seat, put his hand on the controller and felt his heart beating faster. A stop appeared on the screen. He braked too late and went twenty metres too far. The instructor laughed. “That happens to everyone on the first day,” he said. “Even to your grandfather, I've heard.”

In the evening, Leo took the M10 along Kastanienallee. He could have gone straight home to Treptow, where his mother was waiting with dinner. But he wanted to go to his grandfather first. He got off at the new step-free stop, next to the little chestnut tree, which was by now one and a half metres tall and whose leaves were already turning a little yellow. Ludwig was sitting, as on almost every evening, on the bench in front of the café “Bei Ingrid”, with Fritz at his feet. Fritz was fourteen now and very slow, but when he saw Leo, he got up and wagged his tail.

Ludwig had read the press release too, of course, three times, with his reading glasses, and then underlined all the nouns ending in “-ung” in pencil. There had been twenty-seven of them, in a text half a page long. He had shown them to Elif, and Elif had asked whether the people at the BVG didn't like verbs.
Well? How did the carrying out of your first day of training go? Did the commissioning take place successfully?

Leo laughed so loudly that two customers in the café turned round. Then he sat down next to his grandfather and told him everything: about Wolff's speech, about the woman from Ghana, whose name was Abena, about the former baker, about the simulator and the twenty metres too far. Ludwig listened without interrupting. When Leo had finished, he said: “With me it was fifty metres. On the first day. With a real tram, not a simulator. And with sixty passengers inside, who all got off and had to walk back to the stop. Mr Pohl didn't speak to me for a week.”

“And then?” Leo asked. Ludwig smiled. “Then he took me with him again, the following Monday, and made me practise ten times at every stop. Start, brake, start, brake. Until I stopped to the centimetre. He said: a driver who goes too far is annoying. A driver who brakes too early is dangerous. But a driver who learns nothing from his mistakes has no business in a tram.” He patted Leo on the knee. “Today you learned twenty metres. Tomorrow you'll learn ten. Next week five. And at some point you'll stop exactly where the people are standing.”

Later Andrei came out of the house, with his laptop under his arm and a tired, happy face. His app had been available to all passengers for two weeks. Fifty thousand people had already downloaded it. The BVG press release said: “As a result of the introduction of accessible passenger information, a significant increase in use by persons with reduced mobility is being recorded.” Andrei had read the sentence three times and then asked Lena what it meant. Lena had said: “It means more people like Grandpa are taking the tram again. And that you're a hero. But of course they don't put it like that.”

Andrei sat down next to them on the bench, and Fritz immediately laid his head on his foot. He told them about an email he had received that afternoon. A seventy-eight-year-old woman from Spandau, with two hip replacements, had written that for the first time in five years she had visited her sister in Köpenick on her own. By tram. Without help. Because the app had told her which tram was coming without steps and at which stop she could change without climbing a staircase. At the end there was a sentence Andrei knew by heart: “I don't know who you are. But you've given me my sister back.”

Lena had printed out the email and hung it on the wall next to the till in the café, right next to the brass bell. Underneath she had written in chalk: “Our hero works at the BVG.” Andrei went red every time a customer read it. But he hadn't taken it down.

The three of them sat on the bench for a long time, two young men and an old one, with an old dog between them, and watched the trams stopping at the new stop and moving on, stopping and moving on, with their lit windows in the dusk. At some point Leo said: “Grandpa, in three years I'll come past here. With my tram. Then I'll ring twice. So you know it's me.” Ludwig said nothing. He just nodded. But Andrei, who was sitting next to him, saw that he had taken the old brass bell out of his jacket pocket and was holding it tight, very tight, as if he wanted to start practising already.
